item.title: New York City recovers $131 million from DoorDash for delivery workers
item.description: The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) has reached a settlement of $131.5 million with DoorDash for violating local delivery worker laws. More than 260,000 workers were underpaid, with some receiving no payment at all or being paid late. Over $115 million will go directly to delivery workers, plus $16 million in fines and costs. item.title: Nike founder Phil Knight donates $1 billion to University of Oregon
item.description: Phil Knight, co-founder of Nike, has made a $1 billion gift to his alma mater, the University of Oregon, together with his wife Penny. According to the New York Times, this is the largest single donation ever made to an American public university. item.title: Orphaned rhino Tytan and zebra Notty inseparable after losing their mothers
item.description: At the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust in Nairobi, which has been caring for injured and orphaned animals in East Africa since 1977, a special bond formed between two young animals. item.title: Ghana cuckoo-shrike resurfaces in Ivory Coast after 13 years
item.description: Researchers Paulo Ditzel and Stephanie Bartlett of the International Bird Conservation Partnership (IBCP) have spotted the Ghana cuckoo-shrike (Lobotos lobatus) again, in Taï National Park in Côte d'Ivoire. The last confirmed sighting of this striking orange-yellow-black bird dated from 2013, in the Atewa forest in Ghana. During a bird count, Ditzel spotted the bird among a group of other species.

item.title: Nonprofit Rise Up trains formerly incarcerated men as machinists
item.description: In a converted workshop in Southeast San Diego, the nonprofit Rise Up Industries teaches men who spent decades in prison the trade of machinist. The program combines paid apprenticeships with therapy and case management. The workshop fulfills orders for aerospace, medical equipment, auto parts, and fishing lures, among others. item.title: World record: largest beaver dam hidden in Wood Buffalo National Park
item.description: In Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, an area as large as Switzerland, lies the world's largest beaver dam. The dam was only discovered in 2007 through satellite imagery by landscape ecologist Jean Thie; park managers had no knowledge of it until then. item.title: Reading for pleasure protects the brain against dementia
item.description: A new review by researchers from Cambridge University shows that reading for pleasure, whether from an old paperback or an e-reader, is linked to better memory and attention, fewer mental health problems, and a significantly lower risk of dementia. These findings apply to all age groups: you don't need to have been an avid reader as a child to benefit...

item.title: Ethiopians plant millions of trees via Green Legacy Initiative
item.description: Ethiopia lost around 560,000 hectares of forest between 2000 and 2025 to agriculture, logging and charcoal production. In 2019, the government launched the Green Legacy Initiative, which saw citizens planting trees on a massive scale. Yitebitu Moges of UNEP's REDD+ programme says that even if only half the trees survive, there are already gains for moisture, soil and carbon storage....

item.title: Livestream captures wildlife at remote waterhole in Watarrka
item.description: At Australia's Watarrka National Park, a camouflaged camera livestreams a remote desert waterhole to the world. Positioned 1.2 miles from the nearest parking area, the camera captures dingoes, wallabies, frogs, feral cats and even a wedge-tailed eagle as they come to drink. The project was established by Northern Territories Parks and Wildlife and the Research Institute for the Environment and...

item.title: New wild cat species tilcayo discovered in Bolivia
item.description: A new wild cat species has been confirmed in the Yungas cloud forest in Bolivia: the tilcayo, scientifically named Leopardus tilcayo. For years, the spotted animal was regarded as an ordinary ocelot, but local communities had always called it by a different name. item.title: South Korea recycles 97 percent of all food waste
item.description: In Seoul, Seunghwan Hong tosses his food scraps into a smart waste bin: he taps his card, the bin weighs the waste and he pays by weight. This is how South Korea's food waste recycling rate climbed from 2.6 percent in 1996 to nearly 97 percent in 2023, thanks to volume-based fees (1995), mandatory separation (1997), a landfill ban (2005)...

item.title: Portuguese cork firm insulates spacecraft
item.description: Portuguese company Corticeira Amorim, which has existed for 150 years, processes cork oak into sustainable high-tech materials. The cork oak forests of Herdade Rio Frio thrive in the Mediterranean climate and provide usable bark for up to 200 years, with each tree harvested nine times after 25 years. item.description: A group of teenage environmental activists from California, united under the name Another Bounce and working with the organization Habits of Waste, has set a Guinness World Record for the most racket sport balls recycled in a single day. item.description: On September 21, two fishermen spotted a trunk above the water of the swollen Teesta River in West Bengal, India. It turned out to be an elephant calf that had been swept nearly five kilometers downstream after attempting to cross the river. item.title: Orphaned elephant Kipekee rescued after days alone in Kenya
item.description: On June 17, 2025, a four-week-old elephant calf was found among a farmer's livestock near the Maasai Mara National Reserve in Kenya. She was exhausted and malnourished after wandering alone for three days. Rangers from Pangolin Project and Mara Elephant Project discovered her just before she collapsed. item.title: Bicycles beat cars during rush hour on Leith Walk in Edinburgh
item.description: For the first time in history, there were more cyclists than cars on Leith Walk, one of Edinburgh's longest streets, between 8 and 9 in the morning. This emerges from a 48-hour traffic survey conducted by Cycling Scotland across urban Scotland in May. Bicycle trips surged to 67,000 that weekend, a 25% increase compared to the previous year. item.description: Gut bacteria that break down compounds from pomegranates, walnuts and berries produce a metabolite called urolithin A. item.title: Reefvive builds coral reef from oyster shells
item.description: Students from National Taiwan Normal University have developed Reefvive: an artificial reef made from ground oyster shells and coral rubble, materials normally discarded. The waste is processed into a mixture that is 3D-printed into a modular base with a rough surface where young coral can attach. item.title: Araticum Initiative restores 4.4 million acres of Cerrado savanna in Brazil
item.description: The Araticum Initiative in Brazil has been recognized by the UN as one of the three most ambitious and impactful restoration projects in the world. It focuses on the Cerrado, the world's most biologically rich savanna, half of which has already been cleared or converted for agriculture or other uses.
